name: Anglo-Oriental studio pottery
summary: British studio pottery that Bernard Leach started at St Ives in 1920. A potter made high-fired stoneware by hand, with ash and iron glazes after Chinese, Korean and Japanese pots.

philosophy.core_thesis: A good pot joins the plain beauty of East Asian stoneware with the English craft of one person who makes, glazes and fires it.
design_principles: Make each pot by one potter from clay to kiln, and sign it with a seal.
Throw the form on the wheel in a plain shape: a round belly, a firm foot and a thick rim.
Cut the foot with a clear bevel of 3 to 5 mm and leave part of it bare.
Use ash, tenmoku and celadon glazes, fired high in reduction at 1280 to 1300 °C.
Paint the decoration with iron or cobalt in a few brush strokes: a leaf, a fish, a bird.
Fire in a wood-fired climbing kiln with a long reduction; accept the variation that results.
Keep the colour to browns, greens and greys of the earth.
Make useful pots first: bowls, bottles and jars for the table.
anti_patterns: Thin porcelain with a clear glaze
Pottery made only to look rustic, with no skill

form.shape: Bowls, tall bottles, round lidded jars, vases and large dishes with a strong, plain shape.
form.profile: A round, full belly with a firm shoulder; a bottle has a narrow neck, and a bowl has a thick rim and a steep wall.
form.foot_and_rim: A trimmed foot ring cut with a bevel and left bare, so that the clay shows; the rim is thick and slightly uneven.
form.proportion: Height 10 to 40 cm; the wall is 4 to 8 mm and the foot one third of the width of the pot.
rules: Throw with a firm hand and leave the finger marks on the belly.
Trim the foot cleanly and keep it bare of glaze.
Let the glaze run thin on the shoulders and pool in the hollows.

bodies.rule: Use a grey or buff English stoneware that fires at 1280 °C and takes ash glaze well. Use earthenware only for slip-trailed pieces of the older English kind.

methods: brush decoration with iron and cobalt
wood-ash glaze mixing by the potter
forming.joins: Handles are pulled and fixed with slip; lids are thrown from the same clay as the jar.
forming.details: Throwing rings, a brush stroke of iron, a bare bevelled foot, spur marks of the kiln and a seal mark of the potter.

glaze.pattern: A few quick brush strokes of iron under an ash glaze: a leaf, a fish or a bird; a plain tenmoku with a rust-brown rim.
glaze.gloss: Satin to gloss, 20 to 60 GU; tenmoku is a deep gloss at 70 GU.
glaze.wear: Ash glaze stays hard and keeps its colour; iron decoration and bare feet darken with use.

palette.strategy: The colours of earth and plants: ash green, iron brown and slate grey, with a little cobalt.

firing.kiln: A wood-fired climbing kiln of Japanese type, with several chambers and a long reduction.
processes: dipping and pouring of the ash glaze
brush painting of iron and cobalt
firing.scale: A small pottery of 5 to 10 workers; each firing holds about 2 000 pots.
firing.signs: Spur marks, an uneven glaze with runs and pools, a bare bevelled foot and a potter's seal.

pieces.form: Tall vase with a plain belly and a leaf painted in iron under ash glaze
Round bottle with a narrow neck and a deep tenmoku glaze
Lidded jar with a thrown lid and a pale green celadon glaze
Wide bowl with a thick rim and a fish painted in wax resist
Slip-trailed English baluster jar with a lead glaze

positive: ash glaze with iron brush painting

evidence.title: Porcelain vase by Bernard Leach, York Museums Trust
Soup bowl from the Leach Pottery

emotion.target_response: A feeling of calm and honest work: the viewer sees a plain, earthy pot and feels that one person made it.

use_cases: a hand-thrown stoneware bowl or bottle
an ash or tenmoku glaze brief
a museum label on British studio pottery
avoid_when: the brief needs identical factory forms

modifiers.how: Use local clay, thick brushwork and a plain strong form; fire in a Japanese climbing kiln.
Alter the thrown form by cutting, tearing and stacking; drop the use of a table.
